top.line: A permission prompt without its reason is weak
top.para: On 7 October 2026 an agent prompt asked to add a repository, showing owner, repository and access but not which session asked or why. The article reads it through the Agent Behaviour Policy, legal precedent on uninformed decisions, past prompt fixes and Anthropic's approval figures, and proposes a why card that carries its reason.

s0.line: The prompt asked for a decision, withholding the reason
s0.para: Decline broke a task with no account of what broke; Allow made the person author of a decision they could not judge. Read through the policy, a prompt is a grant change. Law mostly puts the duty on the asker, the fixes that worked put the why in the prompt, and the proposal is a why card.

s1.line: The prompt showed three fields and no reason
s1.para: The prompt read: add repository SGit-AI__Website, owner SGit-AI, access read, Decline or Allow once. The tool behind it takes only those three values, so there is no reason to show. It did three things right: read not write, host enforcement, and Allow once, yet none is visible as a control.

s2.line: Both buttons carried a cost the prompt never stated
s2.para: The prompt arrived mid-task. Declining derails work the person started, with no word on which step fails or how to resume; allowing makes the person the approver on the strength of a repository name and the word read. A single sentence saying why would have removed both costs.

s3.line: A prompt changes the grant; judge the resulting reach
s3.para: Under the Agent Behaviour Policy the question is what the session becomes once it holds the new access. Read access to a public repository adds little; write access from a session holding confidential data adds an exfiltration path, a risk to be accepted. A boundary enforced by human judgement is only as strong as its information.

s4.line: People approve 93% of prompts and catch few dangers
s4.para: Anthropic reported that sandboxing cut prompts by 84%, users approve 93% of prompts, and 1,053 testers caught a dangerous command 13.6% of the time. Its classifier fails on whether consent covers the blast radius. Answering Checkmarx, Anthropic said users are responsible for reviewing prompts. Preprints show similar rubber-stamping.

s5.line: Law puts disclosure on askers; blame lands on clickers
s5.para: Montgomery, the red hand rule, Interfoto, Berman, Nguyen, GDPR and the EDPB put the duty to give usable information on the one who asks, and token sign-offs do not count as human decisions. Van Gorkom judges deciders on what they could have asked. In practice Elish's moral crumple zone and Horizon show the nearest person takes the blame.

s6.line: Past fixes put the why into the prompt
s6.para: Apple requires purpose strings, Microsoft added number matching and sign-in context after the 2022 Uber push attack, and the CNIL fined Google €150 million and Facebook €60 million so refusing is as easy as accepting. Google OAuth, GitHub and MCP still show no reason. Research shows prompts that cannot be judged get clicked, as with 70.2% of Chrome warnings.

s7.line: A why card states reason, reach, cost and fallback
s7.para: Every field is something the agent already knows: who is asking, why with the instruction quoted, what changes against current reach, what it could cost, what happens if declined, scope and record. Buttons include asking a question first. When the blast radius rises, the card becomes a risk acceptance with a holder, interval and record.

s8.line: The site's own team half does it already
s8.para: The Mandate Stack team asks for decisions with a draft carrying the question, lettered options and an answer box, and its session cards record tools, files and network calls against the mandate. It lacks a required reason on mid-session grant changes; earlier articles cover fixing grants before a session starts instead.

s9.line: Unknown: who asked, configurability, and how the law applies
s9.para: Which session made the request is unknown, since the prompt did not say. The documentation describes no reason field. Anthropic's figures are its own unreplicated studies. None of the cited cases has been applied by a court to an agent permission prompt, and this is not legal advice.

s10.line: Links: the related articles on grants, risk and records
s10.para: Related pieces include Footprint and blast radius, Every risk is already accepted and the risk acceptance vault, The ultimate insider, Why my agents do not run on my laptop, The Mandate Stack, The agent team as it runs, Six agents, one inbox, A personal agent that keeps your secrets and the sandbox brief.

s11.line: Sources: the cases, rules, studies and vendor posts cited
s11.para: Sources include Dinis Cruz's screenshot and voice note of 7 October 2026, Montgomery, Spurling, Interfoto, Berman, Nguyen, GDPR, EDPB and WP251 guidance, SCHUFA, the EU AI Act, Van Gorkom, Hamilton v Post Office, Elish, Apple, Android, Uber, Microsoft, the CNIL, warning research, Anthropic's posts and Checkmarx.
